'''''Sarracenia rubra''''', also known as the '''sweet'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SARU4|taxon=Sarracenia rubra|accessdate=6 November 2015}}</ref> or '''purple pitcher plant''', is a [[carnivorous plant]] in the [[genus]] ''[[Sarracenia]]''. Like all ''Sarracenia'', it is native to the [[New World]]. Its range extends from southern [[Mississippi]], through southern [[Alabama]], the [[Florida panhandle]] and [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]], to the coastal plains of [[North Carolina]] and [[South Carolina]].<ref>[https://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Sarracenia%20rubra.png Biota of North America Program 2014 county distribution map]</ref>

==Morphology and carnivory==

Like other members of the genus ''Sarracenia'', the sweet pitcherplant traps insects using a rolled leaf, which in this species is generally smaller and narrower than most species, usually not exceeding 65 cm (26 inches) in height. ''Sarracenia rubra'' is generally clump-forming. The uppermost part of the leaf is flared into a lid (the [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]]), which prevents excess rain from entering the pitcher and diluting the [[digestion|digestive secretions]] within. The upper regions of the pitcher are covered in short, stiff, downwards-pointing [[trichome|hairs]], which serve to guide [[insect]]s alighting on the upper portions of the leaf towards the opening of the pitcher tube.  The opening of the pitcher tube is retroflexed into a 'nectar roll' or [[peristome]], whose surface is studded with [[nectar]]-secreting glands. Prey entering the tube find that their footing is made extremely uncertain by the smooth, [[wax]]y secretions found on the surfaces of the upper portion of the tube. Insects losing their footing on this surface plummet to the bottom of the tube, where a combination of digestive fluid, wetting agents and inward-pointing hairs prevent their escape. Some large insects (such as [[wasp]]s) have been reported to escape from the pitchers on occasion, by chewing their way out through the wall of the tube.<ref name=laverne>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250092291 Flora of North America, ''Sarracenia rubra'' Walter, 1788.  Sweet or red pitcher plant ]</ref>

==Flowers==
''See also the [[Sarracenia#Flowers and seeds|section on ''Sarracenia'' flowers]] in the main article''.

In [[spring (season)|spring]], the plant produces small, bright red [[flower]]s with five-fold [[symmetry]]. The red [[petal]]s are long and strap-like, and dangle over the [[umbrella]]-like style of the flower, which is held upside down at the end of a 50 cm long [[Scape (botany)|scape]]. The [[carpel|stigmata]] of the flower are found at the tips of the 'spokes' of this umbrella. Pollinating insects generally enter the flower from above, forcing their way into the cavity between the petals and umbrella, and depositing any pollen they are carrying on the stigmata as they enter. The pollinators generally exit the flower, having been dusted with the plant's own pollen, by lifting a petal. This one-way system helps to ensure [[cross pollination]]. ''Sarracenia rubra'' flowers are generally sweet-scented, hence the common name.<ref name=laverne/>

==Growth cycle==

This species is characterised by producing quite floppy pitchers in spring with large wings, perhaps as a method of producing a large surface area of tissue in order to rapidly photosynthesise at the start of the year. Later on in summer and autumn, much more substantial pitchers are produced.{{citation needed|date=December 2025}}

[[File:Sarracenia rubra ssp jonesii.jpg|thumb|right|130px|''S. rubra'' ssp. ''jonesii'']]

==Taxonomy==

''Sarracenia rubra'' taxonomy is rather complicated and still much debated. Currently, there are six subspecies:

*''S. rubra'' subsp. ''rubra'' – the sweet, red-flowered pitcher-plant<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ecos.fws.gov/ecp/species/1574|title=Sweet, red-flowered pitcher-plant (''Sarracenia rubra rubra'')|website=Environmental Conservation Online System|publisher=U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service|access-date=18 December 2025}}</ref>
*''S. rubra'' subsp. ''jonesii'' [=''S. jonesii''] – the mountain sweet pitcherplant, federally protected as an [[Endangered Species Act of 1973|endangered species]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ecos.fws.gov/ecp/species/4283|title=Mountain sweet pitcher-plant (''Sarracenia rubra ssp. jonesii'')|website=Environmental Conservation Online System|access-date=18 December 2025|publisher=U.S. Fish & Wildlife Department}}</ref>
*''S. rubra'' subsp. ''gulfensis'' – the Gulf sweet pitcher plant<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ecos.fws.gov/ecp/species/9941|title=Gulf Sweet pitcherplant (''Sarracenia rubra ssp. gulfensis'')|access-date=18 December 2025|website=Environmental Conservation Online System|publisher=U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service}}</ref>
*''S. rubra'' subsp. ''viatorum''<ref name=rice2018>{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.sarracenia.com/pubs/cpn47-152-159.pdf|title=The Long Overdue Recognition of ''Sarracenia rubra'' subsp. ''viatorum''|last=Rice|first=Barry A.|date=December 2018|magazine=Carnivorous Plant Newletter|volume=47|issue=4|pages=152-159|via=Barry Rice's personal webpage|access-date=18 December 2025}}</ref> – the ancestral pitcherplant<ref name=rice2018/>{{rp|157}}<ref>{{cite web|url=https://explorer.natureserve.org/Taxon/ELEMENT_GLOBAL.2.1152329/Sarracenia_rubra_ssp_viatorum|title=''Sarracenia rubra'' ssp. ''viatorum''|website=NatureServe Network Biodiversity Location Data accessed through NatureServe Explorer|author=NatureServe|publisher=NatureServe|location=Arlington, Virginia|access-date=18 December 2025|date=5 December 2025}}</ref>
*''S. rubra'' subsp. ''alabamensis'' [=''S. alabamensis''] – the Alabama canebrake pitcher plant, federally protected as an endangered species<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ecos.fws.gov/ecp/species/1846|title=Alabama Canebrake Pitcher Plant (''Sarracenia rubra ssp. alabamensis'')|website=Environmental Conservation Online System|publisher=U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service|access-date=18 December 2025}}</ref>
*''S. rubra'' subsp. ''wherryi'' [=''S. alabamensis'' subsp. ''wherryi''] – Wherry's sweet pitcher plant<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ecos.fws.gov/ecp/species/2740|title=Wherry's Sweet pitcher-plant (''Sarracenia rubra ssp. wherryi'')|website=Environmental Conservation Online System|publisher=U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service|access-date=18 December 2025}}</ref>

These placings are somewhat disputed, however, as each could arguably be its own species due to differences in pitcher morphology. The similarity between the flowers of these taxa indicates a close relationship, however.<ref name="D'Amato1988">{{cite book | author=D'Amato P | title=[[The Savage Garden: Cultivating Carnivorous Plants]] | publisher=Ten Speed Press | year=1998 | isbn= 0-89815-915-6 }}</ref>{{page number needed|date=December 2025}}
